appellants: Guna alias Gunasundari and Another … Appellant(s);
respondents: R. Subramanian alias R.S. Mani (Died) and Others … Respondent(s).
sections_referred: Section 2(g) of Pondicherry Hindu Religious Institutions Act, 1972
advocates: For Appellant(s): Mr. V. Kasinatha Bharathi
prayer: Prayer: appeal Suit filed under Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure, praying to set aside the decree and judgment dated 21-7-2011 in O.S. No. 4 of 2010 on the file of The learned Additional District Judge, Puducherry at Karaikal.
judgment_text:
The present first appeal has been filed challenging the decree and judgment dated 21-7-2011 made in the O.S. No. 4 of 2010 on the The learned Additional District Judge, Puducherry, Karaikal.

2. The appellants/plaintiffs filed a Scheme Suit in O.S. No. 4 of 2010 against the 1st respondent/defendant, the deceased Mr R. Subramanian @ R.S. Mani, and the 2nd respondent/defendant, for the efficient administration of Arulmigu Drowbadai Amman Koil. The 1st respondent had died and his legal heirs are impleaded as respondents 3 to 9 to the present appeal.

3. The case of the plaintiffs/appellants in the aforesaid suit was that the temple Arulmigu Drowbadai Amman Koil, was under the administration of one Pakkiam @ Pakkimuthu, husband of the 1st plaintiff/appellant, who had dedicated about 530 kuzhis of land to the temple and was managing its affairs. It was contended that the 1st defendant/respondent who was stranger to the temple, claimed himself to be the trustee and interfered with its administration. Consequently, Pakkiam filed O.S. No. 263 of 1984 for permanent injunction, which was decreed on 5-12-1986 by the principal District Munsif Court, Karaikal, restraining the 1st defendant from doing further damage to the temple properties. Mr Pakkiam thereafter filed a Scheme Suit O.S. No. 40 of 1996, which came to be dismissed following his death. Subsequently the 1st plaintiff/appellant nominated the 2nd plaintiff/appellant to administer the temple as her power agent, and the 2nd plaintiff/appellant has been managing affairs of the temple since then. It's further contended that the 1st defendant falsely claimed ownership over the temple properties, attempted to alienate the same and received amounts from the 2nd defendant, an occupier of the temple land, towards the same. Hence, the aforesaid suit O.S. No. 4 of 2010 has been filed.

4. Per contra, the respondents contended that the 1st respondent is the sole trustee of the said temple and that the plaintiffs have no connection with the temple or its properties. It was submitted that the temple was established by the ancestors of the 1st respondent and has been under their management for generations, and the trusteeship was passed on to the 1st respondent. It was further contended that the 2nd plaintiff was merely an agent of the 1st respondent and had illegally assumed control over the temple's administration. The 1st respondent had also instituted a suit in O.S. No. 34 of 1991 seeking declaration of his status as sole trustee of the temple, which was decreed on 8-9-1992. The respondents further submitted that the 2nd plaintiff, being only a power agent of the 1st plaintiff, is not competent enough to institute the present suit on her behalf. It was also contended that the suit, being one under Section 92 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908, ought to have been instituted before the Principal Civil Court of original jurisdiction. Therefore it was contended that the principal District Judge, Puducherry, alone has jurisdiction to entertain the suit. Hence, the respondents prayed for dismissal of the suit

5. Upon hearing the rival submissions made on either side and upon perusing the evidence on record, the learned District Judge framed the following issues for consideration in O.S. No. 4 of 2010.

(i) Whether this Court has no jurisdiction to try the suit?

(ii) Whether the second plaintiff empowered to file suit in the capacity of the power agent of the first plaintiff?

(iii) Whether the first plaintiff is entitled for a decree as prayed by her in the plaint?

(iv) To what relief the plaintiff is entitled to?

6. The learned District Judge, after hearing the averments advanced from both sides and perusing both the oral and documentary evidence available on record had made the following observations and decided the aforesaid issues. Insofar as Issue 1 is concerned, it was the contention of the defendants that only the Principal Civil Court of Original jurisdiction viz. the principal District Judge, Puducherry, has the appropriate jurisdiction to handle the said suit. The learned District Judge held that the present Court of the principal District Munsif, Karaikal, is a Civil Court of original jurisdiction within the local limits of Karaikal, and therefore, the plaintiff can institute the suit before this Court, and the PDM, Karaikal, has appropriate jurisdiction to deal with the same. As far as Issue 2 is concerned, the learned District Judge noted that the 1st plaintiff had executed a Power of Attorney in favour of the 2nd plaintiff dated 29-10-2004, marked as Ext. A-1. Subsequently the Ext. A-1 clearly substantiates that the 2nd plaintiff, being the power agent of the 1st plaintiff, is authorised to file the suit, verify the plaint, and even appoint an advocate to represent the case. Therefore, the learned District Judge held that the 2nd plaintiff has the power to file the suit on behalf of the 1st plaintiff and to conduct the case. Accordingly, Issues Nos. 1 and 2 were decided in favour of the plaintiffs/appellants.

7. Insofar as Issue 3 is concerned, it was the primary contention of the plaintiffs that the temple was under the administration of one Mr Pakkiam, the deceased husband of the 1st plaintiff, who had dedicated about 530 kuzhis of land to the temple. On the other hand, the defendants contended that the 1st defendant was the sole trustee of the temple. The learned District Judge, after hearing both sides, observed that the plaintiffs had not produced any evidence to substantiate their claim that Mr Pakkiam had dedicated 530 kuzhis of land to the temple. The learned Judge further took note of various litigations between the parties over the years, including O.S. No. 263 of 1984, which was decreed on 5-12-1986, and the copies of the judgment and decree of the same were marked as Exts. A-15 and A16. A perusal of Ext. A-15 shows that the decree in the said suit was directed to be merged with the scheme suit in O.S. No. 40 of 1986, which was subsequently dismissed by judgment dated 8-9-1987, and the copy of the judgment was marked as Ext. A-13. The Ext. A-13 further indicates that the said scheme suit, filed for appointing the deceased Mr Pakkiam as trustee of the temple, was dismissed at the request of the plaintiff's counsel for not taking further steps, from which the learned trial Judge had inferred, that Mr Pakkiam himself was not interested in pursuing the trusteeship in his favour.

8. Further, it was noted that the suits in O.S. No. 26 of 2000 and O.S. No. 4 of 2002 were instituted by the 1st defendant against third parties for eviction. The appeals arising out of the said suits in A.S. Nos. 16 and 26 of 2005 were allowed, which shows that the 1st defendant cannot be treated as the landlord of the suit property and however, the same also does not establish the plaintiffs' claim of trusteeship or administration. The learned trial Judge further took note of Ext. A-2, namely the patta filed by the plaintiffs themselves, which stands in the name of the 1st defendant, who stands as the owner and trustee of the suit properties. Further the plaintiffs had failed to provide any proper Explanation as to how the patta stood in the name of the 1st defendant. Though the 2nd plaintiff, examined as PW 1 and had deposed in cross-examination that he had been administering the temple even prior to 2005 and that the temple stood in the name of the deceased Mr Pakkiam, no documentary proof was produced to substantiate the same. Further, PW 1 admitted in his cross-examination that the patta for the suit property stood in the name of the 1st defendant.

9. The plaintiffs also examined PW 2, who was occupying the temple property, to support their claim. However, PW 2 in her deposition had admitted that the 1st defendant had filed a suit against her restraining her from putting up a thatched roof in her occupation which is situated on the temple property. The learned trial Judge therefore held PW 2 was an interested witness and found her evidence to be unreliable. In light of the above observations made, the learned trial Judge held that the plaintiffs had failed to prove the existence of any trust in the name of the deceased Mr Pakkiam @ Pakkimuthu or his status as trustee of the temple. Consequently, the plaintiffs were held not entitled to the reliefs sought. In view of the findings on Issues Nos. 1 to 3, the learned District Judge dismissed the suit in O.S. No. 4 of 2010 by judgment dated 21-7-2011. Aggrieved by the same, the plaintiffs have filed the present appeal.

10. Heard Mr C. Prabhakaran, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the appellants.

11. The learned counsel for the appellants submitted that the learned District Judge erred in dismissing the suit without properly considering the oral and documentary evidence on record. He contended that several proceedings were pending between the parties, with regard to the disputes arising in the administration of the temple and that the trial court ought to have put an end to the multiplicity of proceedings by decreeing the said suit and framing a scheme for the proper administration of the temple. It was also contended that the learned Judge failed to note that the husband of the 1st appellant, deceased Mr Pakkiam, had earlier obtained an interim injunction against the 1st respondent, and the said proceedings were later clubbed with the scheme suit in O.S. No. 40 of 1986, which came to be dismissed for non-prosecution upon his demise. However, the trial court erroneously held the same as that the plaintiff had shown no interest in assuming trusteeship.

12. The learned counsel further submitted that the appeals in A.S. Nos. 16 and 26 of 2005, arising out of eviction suits filed by the 1st respondent against the 3rd parties, were allowed on the ground that the 1st respondent had failed to establish the jural relationship with the occupants, thereby indicating that he is neither the owner nor trustee of the suit properties. It was also contended that the instant case falls within the purview of Section 2(g) of the Pondicherry Hindu Religious Institutions Act, 1972, and that the trial court ought to have framed a scheme accordingly. He argued that the very existence of the temple is a sufficient proof for the existence of a trust for the administration and management of the temple. He further submits that the finding of the trial court that no documents were produced to prove the existence of the trust is unsustainable, particularly in light of the multiple litigations between the parties.

13. It was also contended that the 1st respondent was attempting to alienate the temple properties without obtaining necessary permission from the competent authorities, and that the 2nd respondent, being an occupant of the temple property, is acting in collusion with the 1st defendant to purchase the same. Therefore the trial court ought not to have relied upon the evidence of respondents deposing as DW 1 and DW 2, who are attempting to appropriate the temple properties. Therefore, in light of the above averments, the learned counsel submits that the learned District Judge ought to have allowed the suit and framed a scheme for the proper management and administration of the temple. He therefore prays that this Court set aside the judgment and decree dated 21-7-2011 passed in O.S. No. 4 of 2010 and allow the present appeal.

14. I have considered the submissions made on the appellants' sides and have perused both the oral and documentary evidence available on record.

15. It can be seen that Issues Nos. 1 and 2 has been decided by the trial court in favour of the appellants. Since the respondents has not entered an appearance to adjudicate the present appeal, this court finds no necessity to re-examine the said issues. Accordingly, this Court is required to adjudicate only Issue 3, namely, whether the 1st appellant in the present appeal is entitled to the relief sought by her in the suit.

16. The primary contention of the appellants is that Late Mr Pakkiam @ Pakkiamuthu, husband of the 1st appellant, was administering the temple and its properties, and had dedicated about 530 kuzhis of land to the said temple. However, the 1st defendant claims to be the sole trustee of the temple, and both parties have been engaged in prolonged litigation over the suit property and its administration.

17. On considering the oral and documentary evidence available on record, it is evident that existence of any trust in the name of Late Mr Pakkiam @ Pakkiamuthu has not been substantiated by the appellants. No evidence has been produced to establish that he was in charge administering or managing the temple and its properties. In the absence of any such proof, this Court is of the considered view that the appellants are not entitled to the reliefs sought in the suit.

18. Accordingly, the judgment and decree dated 21-7-2011 passed by the principal District Munsif Court, Karaikal, is confirmed, and the appeal suit stands dismissed, however with liberty to the appellants to avail the remedies as available under law. Consequently, the connected miscellaneous petition is also closed. No costs.
